title: Fewest Hops to the Last Square
statement:
A row of squares is numbered from 0. You start on square 0. Standing on square i, you may hop forward by any whole number of squares from 1 up to hops[i].

The input is built so that the last square can always be reached. Return the fewest hops needed to land on it. If the row has one square, you are already there and the answer is 0.

examples.why: 0 → 2 → 6. Taking the longest hop first (to square 3) leaves you crawling one square at a time: 4 hops. A shorter hop to the 4 is better.
0 → 3 → 5. Hopping to the biggest number in range (the 3 on square 1) costs 3 hops. What matters is how far a square reaches, i + hops[i], not hops[i] alone.
One hop of length 4. A hop may be shorter than hops[i], so a value that points past the end still finishes in one hop.

constraints: The last square is reachable from square 0
hints: Group the squares by how many hops it takes to reach them. What shape does each group have?
With 0 hops you reach square 0. With 1 hop you reach a solid block right after it. The block for k + 1 hops ends at the farthest i + hops[i] over the squares of block k.
Walk left to right, tracking the end of the current block and the farthest reach seen inside it. Each time you walk past the end of the current block, you must spend one more hop.

explain.intuition:
This is a breadth-first search, but the layers are solid blocks, so you never need a queue. Layer 0 is square 0. Layer 1 is every square one hop away: the block up to hops[0]. In general, layer k + 1 runs from just after layer k up to the farthest i + hops[i] among the squares in layer k. The answer is the number of the layer that contains the last square.

Why it never hurts to jump to the square that reaches farthest: compare any two squares a and b in the same layer with a + hops[a] ≥ b + hops[b]. Every square that b can reach next, a can reach too, since the reachable squares from both are blocks ending at those values. So swapping b for a in any plan keeps the number of hops the same or makes it smaller. The tempting wrong rules pick by hop length or by hops[i]; the exchange argument says the only number that matters is i + hops[i].
steps: Set hopsUsed = 0, end = 0 (end of the current layer) and far = 0.
For i from 0 to n − 2: far = max(far, i + hops[i]).
If i == end, you have scanned the whole layer: hopsUsed++ and end = far.
Return hopsUsed. The loop stops before the last square, because standing on it needs no further hop.
pitfalls: Looping all the way to n − 1. When the last square is exactly the end of a layer, you count one hop too many; on [0] you return 1 instead of 0.
Hopping as far as possible from each square. Example 1 needs 4 hops that way instead of 2.
Choosing the next square by the largest hops[i]. Example 2 shows the position counts too.

solutions.title: Fewest hops to every square
solutions.idea: dp[i] is the fewest hops to square i. From each square, update every square its hop covers.

solutions.title: Breadth-first layers as blocks
solutions.idea: The squares reachable in exactly k hops form a block. Scan each block once, remembering the farthest reach inside it; that is where the next block ends.

followups: Return the squares you land on, not just the count.
Each hop now has a cost equal to its length squared. Does any greedy still work?
